steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on predicting the type of a UAV from its flight logs with an LSTM, exploring sampling and data augmentation for time series classification. Motivate the problem, explain why type prediction matters, outline our approach and contributions, and give the paper's organization.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have become more and more popular recently because they are compact, have low weight, are easy to use and have good maneuverability. Apart from military applications, civilians also use UAVs a lot, for construction, agriculture, cinema, and conservation. But these good applications come with the opportunities UAVs give for malicious actions. For example UAVs can be used with low risk to enter places like airports, prisons and government buildings. In prisons, UAVs can be used to bring in contraband like phones or drugs. As people use and rely on UAVs more, the potential for misuse also grows.

It is hard for an outside observer to tell if a UAV is behaving properly, maliciously, or is malfunctioning. Machine learning can help with this. Most of the current research focused on identifying anomalous UAV behavior. These approaches work well as long as all the anomalous behaviors of interest are in the training data. But existing machine learning models miss a key aspect, which is determining what potential threat a UAV poses.

To do a threat assessment of a UAV, we first have to identify the characteristics of the airframe. Then we can use these characteristics to predict what the UAV is capable of. For example a fixed-wing UAV can carry more and travel farther. More weight can mean a larger threat, whether the payload is explosives, signals intelligence equipment, or illegal drugs. Identifying the UAV type has several benefits compared to only detecting anomalies. First, with type detection we can learn from more UAV flight data sets, and not only the ones where anomalous behaviors are identified. Training with multiple datasets that are readily available, maybe in combination, can make the model more useful. Second, if we know the type of UAV it can help with other machine learning predictions, for example using the flight characteristics of the UAV to predict its future positions.

- Our approach
  - LSTM to predict UAV type; effect of preprocessing and sampling the time series
  - LSTM: whole-sequence prediction via feedforward and feedback loops
  - PX4 Flight Review, one of the largest public UAV flight log repositories, for a baseline
  - challenges: ten years of collection, changing UAVs and process; serious type imbalance
  - first to predict UAV type from flight logs
- Contributions: LSTM model; exploration of sampling methods; experiment on sampling, configuration, data augmentation
- Organization: Sections II-VIII (related work, PX4 data and three types, methodology, training, experiments, results, limitations); supplemental paper at https://osf.io/mnsgk/

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have become more and more popular recently because they are compact, have low weight, are easy to use and have good maneuverability. Apart from military applications, civilians also use UAVs a lot, for construction, agriculture, cinema, and conservation. But these good applications come with the opportunities UAVs give for malicious actions. For example UAVs can be used with low risk to enter places like airports, prisons and government buildings. In prisons, UAVs can be used to bring in contraband like phones or drugs. As people use and rely on UAVs more, the potential for misuse also grows.

It is hard for an outside observer to tell if a UAV is behaving properly, maliciously, or is malfunctioning. Machine learning can help with this. Most of the current research focused on identifying anomalous UAV behavior. These approaches work well as long as all the anomalous behaviors of interest are in the training data. But existing machine learning models miss a key aspect, which is determining what potential threat a UAV poses.

To do a threat assessment of a UAV, we first have to identify the characteristics of the airframe. Then we can use these characteristics to predict what the UAV is capable of. For example a fixed-wing UAV can carry more and travel farther. More weight can mean a larger threat, whether the payload is explosives, signals intelligence equipment, or illegal drugs. Identifying the UAV type has several benefits compared to only detecting anomalies. First, with type detection we can learn from more UAV flight data sets, and not only the ones where anomalous behaviors are identified. Training with multiple datasets that are readily available, maybe in combination, can make the model more useful. Second, if we know the type of UAV it can help with other machine learning predictions, for example using the flight characteristics of the UAV to predict its future positions.

In this paper we use a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model to predict the type of UAV flown, and we explore how different ways of preprocessing and sampling the time series affect the performance of the model. The LSTM model has particular advantages for classifying UAV type. We can input time series data and it makes classification predictions based on the whole sequence by using feedforward and feedback loops. Good predictions need a lot of data, so we use one of the largest public repositories of UAV flight logs, PX4 Flight Review, to establish a prediction baseline. This dataset has its own challenges for machine learning. It was collected over ten years and the UAVs used and the collection process changed a lot in that time. Also, the number of UAVs for each type is seriously imbalanced. Later in the paper we describe how we dealt with these challenges and trained an effective LSTM model for classifying UAV type. As far as we know our work is the first to predict UAV type from flight log information.

The contributions of this paper are:

- 1. An LSTM predictive model that classifies well the type of UAV flown in a general-purpose flight log,

- 2. An exploration of the sampling methods that are available for time-series trajectory-based classification, and

- 3. The results of an experiment about how different sampling, configuration and data augmentation approaches affect model performance.

The paper is organized like this. Section II reviews the literature about UAV type prediction, and also the adjacent fields of maritime anomaly detection and time series classification. In Section III we detail the PX4 data we use and the differences between three key UAV types, quadrotors, hexrotors and fixed-wing (see fig. 1 for an illustration of these drones). Section IV is about our methodology for classifying these types, including how we construct the machine learning model and the data engineering. Section V explains how to train the model. After that we describe the experiments for evaluating model performance (Section VI), we analyze and discuss the results (Section VII), and we address the limitations of our approach (Section VIII). We also have a supplemental paper with more tables and figures in a public repository (https://osf.io/mnsgk/).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have been increasing in popularity recently due to their compact size, low weight, ease of use, and good maneuverability. Beyond military applications, UAVs are also widely used by civilians for construction [1], agriculture [2], cinema [3], and conservation [4]. These beneficial applications are counterbalanced by the opportunities UAVs create for malicious actions. For instance, UAVs can be used with low risk to enter areas like airports, prisons, and government buildings [5,6,7]. In prisons, UAVs can be used to bring in contraband such as phones or drugs. As the use of and reliance on UAVs increases, so does their potential for misuse.

For an outside observer, it is difficult to tell whether a UAV is behaving properly, behaving maliciously, or malfunctioning. Machine learning can help with this task. Most current research has focused on identifying anomalous UAV behavior [8,9,10]. These approaches work well as long as the training data shows all anomalous behaviors of interest. However, a key aspect missed by existing machine learning models is determining the potential threat a UAV poses.

To perform a threat assessment of a UAV, we must first identify the characteristics of the airframe. We can then use these characteristics to predict the UAV's capabilities. For instance, a fixed-wing UAV can carry more and travel farther. Whether the payload is explosives, signals intelligence equipment, or illegal drugs, more weight can indicate a larger threat. Identifying the type of UAV has several benefits over detecting anomalies alone. First, type detection allows learning from more UAV flight data sets, not only those with identified anomalous behaviors. Training with multiple readily-available datasets, possibly in combination, can improve the utility of the model. Second, knowing the type of UAV can help with other forms of machine learning prediction, such as predicting its future positions from its flight characteristics.

In this paper, we use a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model to predict the type of UAV flown and explore how different approaches to preprocessing and sampling the time series affect model performance. The LSTM model is particularly well suited to UAV type classification: it takes time series data as input and makes classification predictions based on the entire sequence through feedforward and feedback loops. As good predictions require considerable data, we use one of the largest public repositories of UAV flight logs—PX4 Flight Review—to establish a prediction baseline. This dataset poses its own challenges for machine learning. It was collected over ten years, during which the UAVs used and the collection process changed substantially. Moreover, the data has a serious imbalance in the number of UAVs of each type. Later in the paper we describe how we addressed these challenges and trained an effective LSTM model for UAV type classification. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to predict UAV type from flight log information.

This paper makes the following contributions:

- 1. An LSTM predictive model that effectively classifies the type of UAV flown in a general-purpose flight log,

- 2. An exploration of the sampling methods available for time-series trajectory-based classification, and

- 3. The results of an experiment on how varied sampling, configuration, and data augmentation approaches affect model performance.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the literature related to UAV type prediction, including the adjacent fields of maritime anomaly detection and time series classification. In Section III we detail the PX4 data we use and the differences between three key UAV types: quadrotors, hexrotors, and fixed-wing (see fig. 1 for an illustration of these drones). Section IV covers our methodology for classifying these types, including machine learning model construction and data engineering. We explain how to train the model in Section V. We then describe our experiments for evaluating model performance (Section VI), analyze and discuss the results (Section VII), and address the limitations of our approach (Section VIII). Lastly, a supplemental paper with additional tables and figures is available in a public repository (https://osf.io/mnsgk/).
